Companies nowadays in these programming fields apparently like big-O languages. Though you don't technically need to learn calculus and such. The reason you might want to learn Linear Algebra is specifically for memory block and allocations. Hence the object orientation.
To paint you a picture. Think of it like this:
Memory is a series of transistors put together. Most cases they'll teach you at 8086 chip sets, which have 32-bit memory, or in the hardware form is a 32 registry memory block. To find the maximum amount of value that can hold you take 2 to the power of registries, which would yield about 2*2,147,xxx,xxx or about 4.3 gigabytes of memory. But each "Byte" consists of 8 bits which those in itself are transistors.
This is where matrix operations kind of help, since memory is allocated in a form of a matrix.
For example, I want my CPU an 8086 chip to call upon the address, 01x0000FF (give or take that be the address) it's calling upon spot 255 at line 1. Now comes where I want to MOVR1toR5, which means to move Register 1 data to Register 5, or such.
Of course this is the hardware being controlled thru software. But now, instead of that, I want to create a "class" or an object, lets call it "Introductory"
When creating this class, your compiler will declare a certain amount of space in your RAM.
Now, this is why you usually want to declare a form of ticker to use commands like RAND/srand and such.
In C/C++ this command looks like srand(time(0))%x "%" being the modulo symbol, x being the number of clock count/state counters you want to reserve.
I want to declare an integer, usually in many cases if integer is not declared a bit-size it'll go to 1-byte by default, which does not include sign bits, or decimal bits. (This is where Discrete mathematics would come in) though it is not necessary to understand this concept. I declare int x = 0. Which I now have assigned a 1-byte integer x = 00000000.
But now, I want a case where x = rand%8; which tells the program to generate a random number (RNGesus)
but also I have to declare where this is generating from, SO, srand(time(0)) tells the program that it wants it to come from the clock at timestamp 0. So whatever value the memory holds at time 0 will output the value. Something like that.
You'll see much more of this when you decide to take on Big-O programs, though Math does not have to be your strongest point, it does help you see what to do with your psuedocode when you decide to start programming.

What made Kubrick such a great director? An excellent article with amazing fanart

Given the fact that Kubrick was a cinematic genius, it would take a book to offer all the reasons for why he was such a great director. Primarily, though, his greatness stems in the purity of his belief in images, more specifically moving images to tell a story. What distinguishes Kubrick from other directors who abide by the same principle, is that he thought like a poet. Every scene he composed, every image in each frame, was there to communicate an idea or evoke an emotion. Nothing appears wasted. A good example of this occurs in his early film, "killer's kiss" where Davy the boxer sits in his room, looking into a mirror, and kubrick cuts to a few photographs that have been pasted on the margins of the mirror. In just a few shots, we have the protagonists back story, all of it told through images and without a word being spoken. Kubrick was already an accomplished photographer for Look magazine by the time he made this film and his attention to detail and composition is what makes his films such a pleasure to watch.
